title: Eigenvalue scatter with unit circle: are the discrete eigenvalues inside the stable disc?
summary: The same stability question as F5.2 seen from the other side: instead of scaled eigenvalues in the z-plane, you plot the eigenvalues mu = R(h lambda) of one time step and check whether they lie inside the unit circle.

media.alt: Complex plane with a shaded unit disc and orange unit circle; blue squares for explicit Euler and teal circles for RK4; dotted rose lines to the points outside the circle.
media.caption: Reference render of class F5.3 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Are the discrete eigenvalues inside the stable disc?
read_the_figure.axes: x: Re(mu). y: Im(mu). Equal aspect. The orange circle is the unit circle |mu| = 1 and the shaded disc is the stable region.
look_at: Which markers are outside the unit circle? Those are the modes that grow.
Do the two methods differ for the same underlying eigenvalue? Which marker is closer to the origin (more damped)?
Where do points sit near the circle: slowly damped modes?
Are the outside points joined to the origin so their magnitude can be read?
as_drawn: Six continuous-time eigenvalues (-1, -3 plus or minus 2i, -0.4 plus or minus 4i, -8) are mapped by h = 0.4 into the plane of mu = R(h lambda).

Blue squares are explicit Euler, teal circles are RK4. Three Euler squares lie outside the circle (|mu| = 1.81, 1.81 and 2.20); the RK4 circles at (0.034, plus or minus 0.79) and so on are inside, but the RK4 point from lambda = -8 is missing in the visible window because it lands at 1.83, outside the plotted limits.
Dotted rose segments join the origin to each unstable Euler point; the label |mu| > 1: unstable sits at the upper left.
The note in the corner states mu = R(h lambda), h = 0.4, so the reader knows what was plotted.
read_the_figure.proves: If every eigenvalue of the one-step map lies strictly inside the unit circle, repeated application decays: the discrete system is asymptotically stable. A single point outside gives a mode that grows without bound.
if_wrong: A point outside the circle: that mode amplifies each step. Reduce h or change method.
Points exactly on the circle: marginal; roundoff and nonlinearity decide. Typical for conservative problems and ideal for a symplectic method.
The window cuts off a point: a missing marker is a hazard. Here the RK4 value from lambda = -8 is outside the visible limits.
must_check: unit circle: the stability boundary for a discrete map is |mu| = 1, so it is the reference every point is judged against.

terms.meaning: The linear map taking the state at step n to step n + 1. For a linear problem it is a matrix whose eigenvalues decide long-run behaviour.
An eigenvalue mu of that matrix. For a Runge-Kutta method on a diagonalisable problem, mu = R(h lambda) for each continuous eigenvalue lambda.
The set of complex numbers of modulus 1; the boundary of the stable region for a discrete map.
The largest |mu|. The map is stable if it is below 1.
Some |mu| equals 1: the solution neither decays nor grows, as for an undamped oscillator.

remember: mu = R(h lambda): the F5.2 plane mapped through the stability function.
Explicit Euler: mu = 1 + h lambda. RK4: mu = R(h lambda).
The distance of mu from the origin is the per-step amplification.
The window must show every point.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Position is mu in the complex plane. Marker shape separates the two methods. The orange circle is the unit circle and the lightly shaded disc inside it is the stable region. A dotted line from the origin to an outside point lets you read its modulus as the length of the line.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Plain language: after one step each mode is multiplied by a complex number mu. If its size is more than 1 the mode grows every step, so growth is simply being outside a circle. Drawing the circle makes a hard algebraic test into a visual one, and it works for any one-step method or matrix, not only Runge-Kutta.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: Eigenvalues describe the long-run behaviour of a linear map; a non-normal matrix can grow a lot transiently even with all |mu| < 1. A point drawn just inside the circle looks safe but decays very slowly. Plotting with unequal aspect ratio turns the circle into an ellipse and invites misreading. A marker outside the axis limits disappears silently.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: The F5.2 stability-region plot answers the question in terms of h lambda, which is more useful for choosing h. For nonlinear problems, track the largest eigenvalue of the Jacobian along the solution instead (F6.1). For non-normal systems, pseudospectra are the honest tool, beyond this page.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Colour each marker by the continuous eigenvalue it came from, draw arrows from the z-plane position to the mu position, and add a second panel with a smaller h so the points can be seen moving inward.

steps.title: From one step to eigenvalues
steps.note: The state decays if and only if the spectral radius is below 1.

steps.title: Mapping the continuous eigenvalues
steps.note: Euler gives 1 + h lambda; RK4 gives the quartic polynomial from F5.2.

steps.title: Per-step amplification
steps.note: For lambda = -3 + 2i and h = 0.4 explicit Euler gives |mu| = |-0.2 + 0.8i| = 0.825 (inside) while lambda = -0.4 + 4i gives |0.84 + 1.6i| = 1.81 (outside).

worked.title: Reading which modes grow in the reference render
worked.problem: From the figure and h = 0.4: (1) Which explicit Euler eigenvalues are outside the circle, and by what factor does each grow per step? (2) Why is the lambda = -8 Euler point at -2.2 unstable while lambda = -1 at 0.6 is not? (3) How does RK4 treat the oscillating eigenvalue near 4i?

solution.text: (1) Three squares are outside: the pair near 0.84 plus or minus 1.6i and the point at -2.2.
They grow by factors 1.81 (a complex pair, so growth with oscillation) and 2.2 (growth with alternating sign) per step.
(2) For real lambda, Euler gives mu = 1 + h lambda, stable only for h lambda between -2 and 0.

(3) RK4 gives mu of about 0.034 plus or minus 0.79i for that mode, modulus 0.79: it is inside the circle and damped, while Euler amplifies the same mode. This is the larger imaginary reach of the RK4 region.

worked.answer: Three Euler eigenvalues are unstable with growth factors 1.81, 1.81 and 2.2; RK4 keeps the oscillating mode inside the circle at modulus about 0.79. RK4's own lambda = -8 value is 1.83 and so would be unstable too, but it lies outside the plotted window.

analyze.q: The RK4 marker from lambda = -8 is missing from the picture. Where would you expect it, and what is the lesson for the plot?
analyze.hint: Compute R(-3.2) and compare with the axis limits.

evaluate.q: Is |mu| < 1 for all modes enough to guarantee a good answer at a given tolerance?

create: Build the same plot for implicit Euler, where mu = 1 / (1 - h lambda), and check that all six points are inside.

checks.q: What does a marker outside the unit circle mean?
checks.hint: Think of multiplying by mu each step.
checks.answer: That mode is amplified by |mu| > 1 every step, so it grows geometrically.

checks.q: Euler with h = 0.25 on lambda = -9. Stable?
checks.answer: mu = 1 - 2.25 = -1.25, modulus 1.25 > 1, so unstable; need h < 2/9 = 0.222.

checks.q: All markers are inside the circle, yet the solution grows temporarily by a factor of 20. Explain.
checks.answer: A non-normal one-step matrix can have large transient growth even with spectral radius below 1, because eigenvectors are nearly parallel; eigenvalues alone do not bound the norm of M^n for small n.
